slides.title: DFS examines descendants before siblings
slides.visibleText:
SELECTION RULE
Remove the deepest frontier state next

When a state is examined, its children and their descendants are examined before its siblings.

STRENGTH

Low memory relative to breadth-first search; it may reach a deep solution quickly.

RISK

It can become lost deep in a graph, loop, or miss a much shorter path in another branch.

IMPLEMENTATION

Place generated children on the left of OPEN, producing stack behavior.

slides.visibleText:
Source trace on the shared graph.

Read one row as an invariant

The leftmost OPEN state is always next. Newly generated children go before older alternatives. CLOSED prevents repeated examination.

PATH RECONSTRUCTION
OPEN and CLOSED alone do not preserve a returned solution path. Store a parent pointer—or an equivalent ancestor structure—for each generated state.

slides.title: BFS explores the space level by level
slides.visibleText:
SELECTION RULE
Remove the shallowest frontier state next

Examine all states at depth n before proceeding to depth n + 1.

STRENGTH

Complete for finite branching and returns a shallowest solution; with equal step costs, that solution is also minimum cost.

RISK

The number of stored frontier states grows exponentially and can make a large space intractable.

IMPLEMENTATION

Place generated children on the right of OPEN, producing queue behavior.

slides.title: A bound prevents infinite descent; deepening removes the guessed bound
slides.visibleText:
DFS WITH A BOUND
Stop a path below a specified depth or time

Treat the cutoff as failure on that path and try another. This is useful in time-limited game search.

DFS WITH DEEPENING
Repeat DFS with bounds 0, 1, 2, …

Each iteration conducts a complete depth-limited DFS to the current bound, then increases the bound by one.

TRADEOFF
Iterative deepening combines shallowest-goal behavior with space on the order of b × d, while repeating work in the upper levels. Its time remains exponential in solution depth.

slides.title: Backtracking pursues a path and recovers from failure
slides.visibleText:
The source backtracking state space.
CLICK IMAGE TO ENLARGE
Continue until goal, dead end, or unacceptable cost

If the goal is found, return the path. At a dead end—or when the current path is too expensive—return to the most recent state with an untried alternative.

IMPORTANT DISTINCTION
DFS already backtracks through its frontier. This list-based variant makes the current path, alternatives, and dead ends explicit and may prune by a path-cost rule; that does not automatically make it heuristic informed search.

BACKTRACK CONDITION
If CS has no children after excluding states already on DE, SL, and NSL, remove states from SL until an available alternative becomes current.
